lessons.title: From Kd to Km: what all the little k's mean
lessons.search: Michaelis Menten kinetics Km Kd explained

blocks.p: Kinetics is just binding plus chemistry. You already know binding from Exam 1: a protein grabs a ligand, and **Kd** tells you how tight that grab is. Now the protein is an enzyme, so after it binds the substrate it actually does something to it. Km is basically Kd with the chemistry step tacked on.

Kd = [E][S]/[ES] = k-1/k1. A **small Kd means tight binding**. Fraction bound is θ = [L]/([L] + Kd), so when [L] equals Kd, exactly half the protein is bound. That's why Kd is the [L] at half-saturation on a fraction-bound curve.

blocks.h: What an enzyme does (and doesn't) change

blocks.p: An enzyme lowers the **activation energy**, the hill between substrate and product. It does **not** change ΔG'°, because ΔG'° only compares where you start and where you end. Dr. Tracy hammered this: you can't get the ΔG of catalysis from ΔG'° = -RT ln K'eq, because that equation never looks at the hill.

Enzymes often move protons around. If **water** (H3O+ or OH-) does it, that's **specific** acid-base catalysis. If an **amino acid side chain** does it, that's **general** acid-base catalysis. The names feel backwards, so just remember: water = specific, amino acids = general. And the local environment can shift a side chain's pKa. Put a positive arginine next to a tyrosine and the tyrosine gives up its proton more easily, so its pKa drops.
The full scheme has six rates (E + S to ES to EP to E + P, forward and back). That's differential-equation territory, so we simplify with five assumptions:

steps: Simple binding: one substrate, one product, no cooperativity like hemoglobin.
Initial rate: [P] is basically zero, so there's no reverse reaction. That kills k-2, and since product release is fast and irreversible, k2 and k3 lump together as kcat.
Steady state: [ES] isn't changing. Rate ES forms, k1[E][S], equals rate ES breaks down, (k-1 + kcat)[ES].
[S] is way bigger than [E], so binding a little substrate doesn't change [S].
Enzyme is conserved: none of it is destroyed or lost along the way.

blocks.tip: These assumptions are only truly valid right at time zero. That's why we measure the initial slope, V0, and nothing later on the curve.

blocks.p: Dr. Tracy's trick: think about the ES complex. Rates that move **away** from ES go on top, rates that move **toward** ES go on the bottom. Away from ES you can either let go (k-1) or do chemistry (kcat). Toward ES there's only binding (k1). So:

blocks.p: Because Km has kcat stuck in the numerator, Km is **not always a pure measure of binding**. A fast enzyme can have a big Km just because it turns substrate over quickly. Km only matches Kd when kcat is tiny compared to k-1.

blocks.h: Three curves that look the same

blocks.p: Fraction bound vs [S] gives you **Kd**. Product vs time gives you **V0** (the initial slope). V0 vs [S] gives you **Vmax** at the plateau and **Km** at half of Vmax. Same shape, different axes. Always read the axes first.

blocks.key: Km = (k-1 + kcat)/k1. Kd = k-1/k1. MM assumptions only hold at the very start, so we measure V0. Enzymes lower the barrier, never ΔG'°.

example.q: k1 = 1 × 10^8 M⁻¹s⁻¹, k-1 = 1000 s⁻¹, kcat = 10,000 s⁻¹. Find Kd and Km.
example.a: Kd = 1000 / 10^8 = 10 µM. Km = (1000 + 10,000) / 10^8 = 110 µM. Km is bigger because the chemistry step adds another way to leave ES.

lessons.title: Vmax, kcat, and catalytic efficiency
lessons.search: kcat Km catalytic efficiency turnover number

blocks.p: Once you have Km and Vmax, you can predict how fast an enzyme runs at any substrate level and compare two enzymes fairly.

V0 = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]). Plug in [S] = Km and you get V0 = Vmax/2, which is the whole definition of Km. When [S] is way below Km, V0 climbs almost in a straight line. When [S] is way above Km, the enzyme is saturated and V0 barely moves. So doubling [S] does **not** double V0 unless you're way down at low [S].

Vmax = kcat[E]total. At saturation every enzyme already has substrate bound, so binding isn't the bottleneck anymore. The only thing limiting speed is the chemistry, kcat. Flip it around and kcat = Vmax / [E]total, the turnover number.

You can't compare enzymes with Km alone or kcat alone. Dr. Tracy's example: enzyme 1 binds great (Km = 1) but reacts slowly (kcat = 1). Enzyme 2 binds poorly (Km = 5) but reacts fast (kcat = 5). Both have kcat/Km = 1. Same efficiency, totally different reasons. Bigger kcat/Km = better overall catalyst.
Kinetically perfect enzymes, like catalase and carbonic anhydrase, have kcat/Km so high that they react basically as fast as substrate can diffuse in. The moment substrate shows up, it's done.

steps: Write V0 = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]).
Keep units matched (mM with mM).
For kcat, divide Vmax by total enzyme.
For efficiency, divide kcat by Km (Km in molar).

blocks.key: V0 = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]); Vmax = kcat[E]total; compare enzymes with kcat/Km.

example.q: Vmax = 100 µM/min, Km = 4 mM. What's V0 at [S] = 12 mM?
example.a: V0 = 100 × 12 / (4 + 12) = 75 µM/min. Tripling [S] past Km only got you from 50 to 75.

example.q: Enzyme A: kcat = 100 s⁻¹, Km = 10 µM. Enzyme B: kcat = 1000 s⁻¹, Km = 500 µM. Which is more efficient?
example.a: A: 100 / 0.00001 M = 1 × 10^7. B: 1000 / 0.0005 M = 2 × 10^6. A wins even though B is faster at saturation.

lessons.title: Reading inhibition: Lineweaver-Burk and the four types
lessons.search: Lineweaver Burk plot competitive uncompetitive mixed noncompetitive inhibition

blocks.p: The MM curve is a hyperbola, which is hard to read by eye. Lineweaver and Burk flipped the equation upside down so it turns into a straight line: 1/V0 = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. That's just y = mx + b.

blocks.tip: The x-intercept is negative 1/Km. If the x-intercept moves closer to zero, -1/Km got smaller in size, which means Km got BIGGER.

blocks.p: Every inhibitor type is just a question of which rate it slows. Vmax = kcat[E]total, so only things that hurt kcat (or remove enzyme) lower Vmax. Km = (k-1 + kcat)/k1, so watch what happens to that fraction.

blocks.p: For mixed, look at where the lines cross. **Above the x-axis** it leans competitive (Km goes up). **Below the x-axis** it leans uncompetitive (Km goes down). Vmax can never go up with an inhibitor, because then it's an activator.

list: If the protein only binds (antibody, hemoglobin, receptor, angiogenin), there's no chemistry to block, so an inhibitor can ONLY be competitive.
Allosteric does not automatically mean noncompetitive. If binding elsewhere warps the pocket so substrate can't bind, that's still competitive.
Transition-state analogs bind tighter than substrate and act competitively.
Suicide (irreversible) inhibitors like aspirin covalently kill the enzyme. LB plots are for reversible inhibitors.
On graph questions, he'll accept your call if you justify it with what happened to Km and Vmax.

steps: Competitive: both curves level off at the same Vmax; the inhibited one rises slower (bigger Km).
Uncompetitive: inhibited curve levels off lower AND hits half of its own max at a smaller [S].
Noncompetitive: inhibited curve levels off lower, but half-max lands at the same [S].
Mixed: lower plateau, and half-max shifts right or left depending on which way it leans.

blocks.key: Competitive: Km up, Vmax same, y-axis cross. Uncompetitive: both down, parallel. Mixed: Vmax down, Km either. Noncompetitive: Km same, Vmax down, x-axis cross.

example.q: LB y-intercept = 0.02 min/µM and x-intercept = -0.25 mM⁻¹. Km and Vmax?
An inhibitor slows only k1. What happens on the LB plot?
example.a: Competitive: Km goes up, Vmax stays the same, so all the lines cross on the y-axis.

questions.question: A receptor has a Kd of 2 µM for its ligand. If the free ligand concentration is 6 µM, what fraction of the receptor (θ) is bound?
questions.explanation: θ = [L]/([L] + Kd) = 6/(6 + 2) = 0.75. Getting 0.25 means you put Kd on top instead of [L].

questions.question: A protein has Kd = 5 µM. What free ligand concentration gets it to 90% bound?
options: 4.5 µM
9 µM
50 µM
45 µM
questions.explanation: Set 0.9 = [L]/([L] + 5) and solve: [L] = 9 × Kd = 45 µM. Each extra 'nine' of saturation costs about 10 times more ligand.

questions.question: Two receptors bind the same hormone. Receptor X has Kd = 0.5 nM and receptor Y has Kd = 50 nM. Which statement is right?
options: X reaches half-saturation at a lower hormone level, so X is the more sensitive receptor
Y reaches half-saturation at a lower hormone level, so Y is the more sensitive receptor
X binds more weakly, because a smaller Kd means the complex falls apart faster
Both are equally sensitive, since Kd only reports how fast binding happens
questions.explanation: Kd is the [L] at half-saturation, so a smaller Kd means tighter binding and a response at lower hormone levels.

questions.question: An enzyme speeds up a reaction a millionfold. What happens to the reaction's ΔG'°?
options: Nothing; the enzyme lowers the activation barrier, but start and end energies stay put
It gets more negative, because the enzyme stabilizes products relative to substrates
It gets more positive, because the enzyme stores some of the energy in the ES complex
It drops by the same amount the activation energy dropped, since the two are linked
questions.explanation: Enzymes change the path, not the destination. ΔG'° only compares substrate and product energies.

questions.question: Dr. Tracy asked if you could get the ΔG of catalysis from ΔG'° = -RT ln K'eq. Why can't you?
options: It only compares substrate and product energies; it never sees the barrier between them
You can, as long as K'eq is measured with the enzyme present instead of without it
You can, but only at standard conditions, where every reactant and product is set to 1 M
That equation only describes binding, so it would give you Kd instead of catalysis
questions.explanation: ΔG'° measures how far 'downhill' the reaction goes overall, not how tall the hill is. Catalysis is all about the hill.

questions.question: An enzyme uses a histidine side chain to pull a proton off its substrate. What kind of catalysis is this?
options: General base catalysis, since an amino acid side chain is the proton acceptor
Specific base catalysis, since one specific residue is the proton acceptor
Specific acid catalysis, since the histidine ends up holding an extra proton
General acid catalysis, since hydroxide from water takes the proton away
questions.explanation: Water (H3O+/OH-) doing the proton work = specific. An amino acid doing it = general. Taking a proton = base.

questions.question: Tyrosine's side-chain pKa is about 10. In an enzyme, a positively charged arginine sits right next to it. What happens to that tyrosine's apparent pKa?
options: It rises, since the nearby positive charge holds the proton tightly onto the tyrosine ring
It drops, since the nearby positive charge stabilizes the negative ring after H+ leaves
It stays at 10, since pKa is a fixed property of each amino acid side chain
It drops, since arginine hands its own proton over to the tyrosine ring
questions.explanation: A nearby positive charge makes the deprotonated (negative) form more comfortable, so the proton leaves more easily. That's a lower pKa.

questions.question: In the enolase example, a Lys and a Glu in the active site were both NEUTRAL at pH 7. Which ways can an active site's local environment make unexpected chemistry possible? (Select all that apply)
options: Changing the reaction's overall ΔG'° so the step becomes favorable
Using bound metal ions (like Mg2+) to stabilize charges that would be unfavorable
Placing charged groups so a residue flips away from its usual charge state
Shifting a side chain's pKa so it's deprotonated when it normally wouldn't be
Raising the pH of the whole cell so every amine gets deprotonated
questions.explanation: The pKa values from the table are for free amino acids. Inside a protein, neighbors and metals shift them. That's how enolase can even pull a proton off a carbon.

questions.question: Which are Michaelis-Menten assumptions? (Select all that apply)
options: [S] is much greater than [E]
Binding the first substrate makes the next one bind more easily
[ES] stays constant over the measurement (steady state)
[P] ≈ 0, so the reverse reaction can be ignored
Total enzyme is conserved through the reaction
One substrate binds and makes one product (simple binding mechanism)
kcat is much larger than k-1 for every enzyme
questions.explanation: Those five are the list from the review sheet. Cooperative binding (like hemoglobin) breaks the 'simple binding' assumption.

questions.question: On a product-vs-time curve, where are the Michaelis-Menten assumptions actually true?
options: Only at the plateau, where product formation has leveled off and stopped changing
Halfway up the curve, where exactly half of the substrate is used up
Only right at the start (time zero), which is why we measure the initial slope V0
Everywhere on the curve, as long as the total enzyme amount stays constant the whole time
questions.explanation: The instant any product forms, [P] isn't zero anymore. So we grab the tangent at the very start and call it V0.

questions.question: Why does assuming [P] ≈ 0 let you drop k-2 (product turning back into substrate)?
options: With no product around, there's nothing to rebind and push the reaction backward
With no product around, the enzyme can't finish catalysis, so k2 drops to zero
With no product around, substrate binding becomes irreversible, so k-1 drops out
With no product around, ES can't form, so the overall rate equals k1 alone
questions.explanation: No product means no Le Chatelier push backward, so the reverse steps (k-2, k-3) disappear.

questions.question: What does the steady-state assumption actually let you set equal to each other?
options: The rate substrate binds, k1[E][S], and the rate product leaves, kcat[ES]
The concentration of free enzyme and the concentration of ES complex
The rate ES forms, k1[E][S], and the rate ES breaks down, (k-1 + kcat)[ES]
The concentration of substrate and the concentration of product at equilibrium
questions.explanation: Steady state means [ES] isn't changing, so formation and breakdown rates match. That substitution is what makes the derivation work.

questions.question: Using the 'away from ES over toward ES' trick, which expression is Km?
options: (k1 + kcat) / k-1
k-1 / (k1 + kcat)
(k-1 + k1) / kcat
(k-1 + kcat) / k1
questions.explanation: Leaving ES: unbinding (k-1) or doing chemistry (kcat). Making ES: binding (k1). Away on top, toward on the bottom.

questions.question: k1 = 1 × 10^8 M⁻¹s⁻¹, k-1 = 1 × 10^3 s⁻¹, and kcat = 1 × 10^4 s⁻¹. What are Kd and Km?
options: Kd = 110 µM and Km = 10 µM
Kd = 10 µM and Km = 100 µM
Kd = 10 µM and Km = 110 µM
Kd = 100 µM and Km = 110 µM

questions.question: When does Km come out about equal to Kd?
options: When kcat is much larger than k-1, so nearly every bound substrate becomes product
When k1 is much larger than k-1, so substrate binds much faster than it comes back off
When kcat is much smaller than k-1, so substrate falls off far more often than it reacts
Never, since Km always carries the extra kcat term on top of Kd's two terms
questions.explanation: Km = (k-1 + kcat)/k1. If kcat is tiny next to k-1, it drops out and you're left with k-1/k1, which is Kd.

questions.question: The review key says Km is 'not always a direct measure of binding affinity.' Why?
options: Km puts k1 on top, so faster binding makes Km bigger even when affinity improves
Km is measured at saturation, so it reflects the maximum rate instead of binding
Km includes kcat, so an enzyme can show a big Km just because its chemistry is fast
Km only applies to inhibitors, so it can't describe how the real substrate binds
questions.explanation: A big kcat inflates the numerator. So a large Km could mean weak binding OR just a really fast chemistry step.

questions.question: Generally, a small Km means the enzyme...
options: Needs a lot of substrate before it really gets going
Has a high turnover number once it's saturated
Binds its product more tightly than its substrate
Works well even when substrate concentration is low
questions.explanation: Km is the [S] where you hit half of Vmax. Small Km = you get there with very little substrate.

questions.question: You see a hyperbola with [substrate] on the x-axis and V0 on the y-axis. What can you read straight off it?
options: Kd as the [S] where half of the enzyme is bound to substrate
V0 as the slope of the steepest early part of the curve
Vmax at the plateau, and Km as the [S] at half of Vmax
kcat at the plateau, and Kd as the [S] at half of kcat
questions.explanation: V0 vs [S] is the Michaelis-Menten plot. Plateau = Vmax, drop down from half of Vmax = Km.

questions.question: Three curves all look hyperbolic. Which pairing of axes and value is right?
options: [S] vs fraction bound gives Kd; time vs [P] gives V0; [S] vs V0 gives Km
[S] vs fraction bound gives Km; time vs [P] gives Kd; [S] vs V0 gives V0
[S] vs fraction bound gives V0; time vs [P] gives Km; [S] vs V0 gives Kd
[S] vs fraction bound gives Kd; time vs [P] gives Km; [S] vs V0 gives V0
questions.explanation: He literally put the same curve up three times and said the only thing that matters is the axes. This was a heavily missed clicker question.

questions.question: If you double [S], does V0 double?
options: Only when [S] is far below Km; as the enzyme fills up, doubling helps less and less
Yes, always, since V0 is directly proportional to substrate concentration
No, never, since V0 depends only on how much enzyme is present
Only when [S] is far above Km, where V0 climbs the fastest as you add more substrate
questions.explanation: Way below Km the curve is nearly a straight line. Near saturation, extra substrate barely moves V0 because every enzyme is already busy.

questions.question: Vmax = 100 µM/min and Km = 4 mM. What's V0 at [S] = 12 mM?
options: 75 µM/min
50 µM/min
25 µM/min
300 µM/min
questions.explanation: V0 = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) = 100 × 12/16 = 75 µM/min. 50 would be the answer only if [S] equaled Km.

questions.question: Vmax = 50 µM/s with 0.010 µM total enzyme. What is kcat?
questions.explanation: kcat = Vmax/[E]total = 50/0.010 = 5,000 s⁻¹. Each enzyme turns over 5,000 substrates per second at saturation.

questions.question: Why is kcat the limit on Vmax?
options: At saturation binding is still the slowest step, so kcat just measures how fast k1 goes
At saturation every enzyme already holds substrate, so only the chemistry step limits speed
At saturation product release stops, so kcat measures how long product stays bound
At saturation the enzyme starts to unfold, so kcat reflects the loss of active enzyme
questions.explanation: Vmax = kcat[E]total. With [S] maxed out, there's no binding left to wait on, only chemistry.

questions.question: Enzyme A: kcat = 100 s⁻¹, Km = 10 µM. Enzyme B: kcat = 1,000 s⁻¹, Km = 500 µM. Which is the better catalyst overall?
options: B, with kcat/Km = 2 × 10^7 M⁻¹s⁻¹ versus 1 × 10^6 for A
B, since its kcat is ten times faster, and kcat is all that matters
A, with kcat/Km = 1 × 10^7 M⁻¹s⁻¹ versus 2 × 10^6 for B
A, since its Km is smaller, and Km is all that matters

questions.question: Enzyme 1 binds well (Km = 1) but reacts slowly (kcat = 1). Enzyme 2 binds poorly (Km = 5) but reacts fast (kcat = 5). What's the takeaway from Dr. Tracy's example?
options: Enzyme 2 is five times more efficient, since fast chemistry always beats tight binding
Enzyme 1 is five times more efficient, since tight binding always beats fast chemistry
You can't compare them, since kcat/Km only works for kinetically perfect enzymes
They have the same catalytic efficiency for different reasons, so you need both numbers
questions.explanation: 1/1 = 5/5 = 1. Binding and chemistry are two separate things, and kcat/Km folds them together.

questions.question: What makes enzymes like catalase or carbonic anhydrase 'kinetically perfect'?
options: Their Km equals their Kd exactly, so binding and catalysis are perfectly matched
Their kcat/Km is so high they react about as fast as substrate can diffuse in
Their Vmax never changes, no matter how much inhibitor gets added
Their ΔG'° is zero, so they push the reaction equally both ways
questions.explanation: Perfect enzymes are limited only by diffusion. The moment substrate arrives, the reaction is basically done.

questions.question: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the y-intercept is 0.02 min/µM and the x-intercept is -0.25 mM⁻¹. What are Vmax and Km?
options: Vmax = 50 µM/min and Km = 4 mM
Vmax = 0.02 µM/min and Km = 0.25 mM
Vmax = 4 µM/min and Km = 50 mM
Vmax = 50 µM/min and Km = 0.25 mM
questions.explanation: y-intercept = 1/Vmax, so Vmax = 1/0.02 = 50. x-intercept = -1/Km, so Km = 1/0.25 = 4 mM.

questions.question: Why did Lineweaver and Burk flip the Michaelis-Menten equation upside down?
options: Plotting 1/V0 vs 1/[S] removes the steady-state assumption, so the math becomes exact
Plotting 1/V0 vs 1/[S] makes the plot work for cooperative enzymes like hemoglobin
Plotting 1/V0 vs 1/[S] lets you see irreversible inhibitors the hyperbola can't show
Plotting 1/V0 vs 1/[S] makes a straight line, so Km and Vmax come right off the intercepts
questions.explanation: Before computers did curve fits, a straight line was the easy way to get Km and Vmax. It's still the clearest way to see inhibitor patterns.

questions.question: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, what does the slope equal?
options: Vmax / Km
1 / Km
-1 / Vmax
Km / Vmax
questions.explanation: 1/V0 = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. The slope is Km/Vmax.

questions.question: An inhibitor slows ONLY k1 (substrate binding). Which trends match?
options: Km goes down and Vmax stays the same; LB lines cross on the x-axis
Km stays the same and Vmax goes down; LB lines cross on the x-axis
Km goes up and Vmax stays the same; LB lines cross on the y-axis
Km and Vmax both go down; LB lines run parallel to each other
questions.explanation: k1 is in the denominator of Km, so a smaller k1 makes Km bigger. kcat is untouched, so Vmax is the same. That's competitive.

questions.question: Why does Vmax stay the same with a competitive inhibitor?
options: Vmax = kcat[E]total, and blocking binding doesn't touch kcat; enough substrate out-competes it
Vmax = k1[E]total, and the inhibitor speeds k1 just enough to cancel its binding effect
Vmax = kcat[S], and the inhibitor lowers [S] by the same amount it raises kcat
Vmax is always measured without any inhibitor, so it can't change no matter what the inhibitor does
questions.explanation: Pile on enough substrate and the inhibitor gets crowded out. Once bound, chemistry runs at full speed.

questions.question: An inhibitor binds somewhere OTHER than the active site, but that warps the pocket so substrate can't bind as well. Whatever does bind reacts normally. What type is it?
options: Competitive, since the end result is blocked binding even though it binds allosterically
Uncompetitive, since anything that binds away from the active site is uncompetitive
Noncompetitive, since allosteric binding pulls enzyme out without changing Km
Mixed, since binding at a second site always changes both Km and Vmax together at once
questions.explanation: The TA notes say it straight: allosteric binding can still be competitive. Ask what it does (blocks binding), not where it sits.

questions.question: In the homework, an inhibitor bound angiogenin (a binding protein, not an enzyme) and blocked it from binding its partner. Why could this ONLY be competitive?
options: Angiogenin is too small for a second site, so the inhibitor has to use the main site
Binding proteins have no Vmax, so mixed or uncompetitive would make Km undefined
Binders like antibodies are always inhibited irreversibly, which counts as competitive
There's no chemistry step to slow down, so the only thing an inhibitor can hit is binding
questions.explanation: No k2 step means uncompetitive and mixed are off the table. Same logic for hemoglobin and BPG, and for receptor antagonists.

questions.question: An inhibitor binds only the ES complex and locks the substrate in, so it can't leave and can't be turned into product. Which trends match?
options: k-1 and kcat drop, so Km and Vmax both drop and the LB lines run parallel
k1 drops, so Km rises while Vmax holds steady and the lines cross on the y-axis
k-1 and kcat rise, so Km and Vmax both rise and the LB lines run parallel
Only kcat drops, so Km holds steady while Vmax drops and lines cross on the x-axis
questions.explanation: Both numerator terms of Km shrink, so Km goes down. kcat drops, so Vmax goes down. Parallel lines are the uncompetitive hallmark.

questions.question: From the TA review: what happens to Km and Vmax if an inhibitor slows the dissociation of the ES complex (traps substrate on the enzyme)?
options: Adding more substrate overcomes the inhibition, so Km ends up larger and Vmax is unchanged
Substrate binding is unaffected, so Km is unchanged and Vmax is smaller than before
Less substrate is needed to hit half of the lowered max rate, so Km and Vmax both get smaller
The ES complex is stabilized, so Km is smaller and Vmax is larger than before
questions.explanation: Trapping ES lowers k-1 and stalls chemistry, which is the uncompetitive pattern. The 'Vmax larger' option is a trap: inhibitors never raise Vmax.

questions.question: With a mixed inhibitor, the LB lines cross to the LEFT of the y-axis and ABOVE the x-axis. What does that tell you?
options: Vmax drops and Km drops, so it leans more like an uncompetitive inhibitor
Vmax drops and Km rises, so it leans more like a competitive inhibitor
Vmax holds steady and Km rises, so it's a purely competitive inhibitor
Vmax rises and Km drops, so the molecule is really acting as an activator
questions.explanation: Crossing above the x-axis = competitive-ish, Km goes up. Below the x-axis = uncompetitive-ish, Km goes down. Vmax drops either way.

questions.question: Noncompetitive inhibition is the special mixed case where...
options: LB lines cross right on the y-axis, so Vmax is unchanged and only Km rises
LB lines run parallel, so Km and Vmax both drop by the exact same factor
LB lines never cross, because the inhibitor removes the enzyme permanently
LB lines cross right on the x-axis, so Km is unchanged and only Vmax drops
questions.explanation: Noncompetitive basically pulls enzyme out of the working pool. Less enzyme = lower Vmax, but the enzyme that's left behaves normally, so Km stays.

questions.question: Which change is IMPOSSIBLE for any of the four reversible inhibitor types?
options: Km going down
Km going up
Vmax staying the same
Vmax going up
questions.explanation: kcat can only stay the same or drop with an inhibitor. If Vmax rises, you've got an activator, not an inhibitor.

questions.question: On a Michaelis-Menten plot, the inhibited curve plateaus lower than the uninhibited one, but both reach half of their own max at about the same [S]. What type is it?
options: Competitive: Vmax is lower and Km is unchanged
Uncompetitive: Vmax is lower and Km is unchanged
Competitive: Vmax is unchanged and Km is higher
Noncompetitive: Vmax is lower and Km is unchanged
questions.explanation: This is the acetazolamide-style graph from class and the TA review: Km same, Vmax smaller = mixed/noncompetitive.

questions.question: Which statements about irreversible ('suicide') inhibitors are true? (Select all that apply)
options: They let go once the drug diffuses away from the enzyme
They show up as a clean set of lines on a Lineweaver-Burk plot
Aspirin is an example; it covalently modifies cyclooxygenase
They usually form a covalent bond with the enzyme
They take that enzyme molecule permanently out of play
questions.explanation: Suicide inhibitors commit the enzyme to a covalent dead end. LB analysis is for reversible inhibitors.

questions.question: A drug is a transition-state analog for its target enzyme. What would you predict?
options: It binds the active site tighter than substrate and acts as a competitive inhibitor
It binds only to the ES complex and acts as an uncompetitive inhibitor instead
It binds the active site weaker than substrate, so it barely inhibits
It binds a separate allosteric site and acts as a noncompetitive inhibitor instead
questions.explanation: Enzymes bind the transition state best of all. A molecule already shaped like it outcompetes the real substrate for the active site.

questions.question: You're told to draw the Michaelis-Menten curves that match LB lines crossing on the y-axis. What should they look like?
options: The inhibited curve levels off lower, but both reach half of their own max at the same [S]
The inhibited curve levels off lower and reaches half of its own max at a smaller [S]
Both curves are identical, since crossing on the y-axis means there's no inhibition
Both level off at the same Vmax, but the inhibited curve rises slower and has a larger Km
questions.explanation: Crossing on the y-axis = same 1/Vmax = competitive. Same plateau, shifted right. He wants you able to convert between the two plots.

lessons.title: How enzymes speed reactions up
lessons.search: how enzymes lower activation energy proximity orientation transition state stabilization

blocks.p: Every enzyme does the same basic job: lower the activation energy so a reaction that was already going to happen can happen fast. Dr. Tracy's peroxide demo showed this. Potassium iodide sped it up about 100-fold, manganese oxide about 1000-fold, and purified catalase could do about a millionfold. Same products, same overall energy change, just different speeds.

head: Strategy
What it means
Size of boost
rows: Bring the reacting groups close together
Hold them in the right angle to react
Restrict random Brownian motion so useful motions win (the ratchet idea)
Bind the transition state better than anything else

blocks.p: **Induced fit** ties into that last one. When substrate binds, the enzyme changes shape around it and pulls the substrate toward the transition state. Enzymes bind the transition state best, which is exactly why transition-state analogs make such good inhibitors.

blocks.key: Proximity and orientation help some; locking down vibrations and stabilizing the transition state are where the big rate boosts come from.

example.q: Which two strategies give the biggest boost?
example.a: Locking down structural vibrations and stabilizing the transition state.

lessons.title: Chymotrypsin step by step
lessons.search: chymotrypsin mechanism catalytic triad oxyanion hole

blocks.p: Chymotrypsin is a serine protease: it uses a serine to cut peptide bonds. Serine's -OH normally has a sky-high pKa, so it should NEVER be a nucleophile at pH 7 or 8. The whole trick is how the enzyme makes it one.

head: Part
Job
rows: Gives specificity: holds the bulky aromatic side chain
Stabilizes the negative oxygen in the tetrahedral intermediate, using backbone N-H groups

blocks.p: The three residues are far apart in sequence (102, 57, 195) but close in 3D, and substrate binding squeezes them even closer. Asp is negative. Sitting next to a negative charge, His really wants to be positive, so its pKa goes up. The closest proton it can grab is on Ser. His pulls it off, and now Ser is an alkoxide, a strong nucleophile. Asp's job is to stabilize the positive His afterward.

steps: The aromatic side chain (Phe, Tyr, Trp) drops into the hydrophobic pocket.
His pulls the H off Ser; the Ser oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon of the peptide bond.
A tetrahedral intermediate forms with a negative oxygen, held in the oxyanion hole.
Electrons come back down, the C-N bond breaks, and His hands its proton to the leaving amine. The amine half of the peptide diffuses away.
Now the carbonyl half is covalently stuck to Ser. This is the acyl-enzyme intermediate (end of phase 1, acylation).
Water slips into the empty space. His pulls a proton off the water, and the water oxygen attacks the carbonyl.
A second tetrahedral intermediate forms in the oxyanion hole.
The bond to Ser breaks, Ser gets its proton back, and the carboxyl half leaves. Enzyme reset (phase 2, deacylation).

blocks.tip: His acts as a general base (taking H from Ser, then from water) and a general acid (giving H to the leaving amine). The oxyanion hole uses the protein BACKBONE, not side chains. He said you don't need to push every arrow, but know the important steps.

blocks.p: A suicide inhibitor can do step 1-5 but never let go: the covalent acyl-enzyme ends up more stable than releasing, so the enzyme is stuck forever.

blocks.key: Triad makes the nucleophile, pocket picks the substrate, oxyanion hole stabilizes the intermediate. Two phases: acylation (amine half leaves) then deacylation (water comes in, carboxyl half leaves).

example.q: What does Asp102 actually do?
example.a: It stabilizes the positive charge on His after His takes Ser's proton. That's what lets His act as a strong enough base.

lessons.title: Pockets, pH, inhibitors, and regulation
lessons.search: serine protease specificity pocket trypsin chymotrypsin elastase

blocks.p: Chymotrypsin, trypsin, and elastase share about 40% of their sequence, the same triad, and nearly the same fold. That's divergent evolution: one ancestor, different jobs. They differ most at the pocket, because that's what picks the substrate.

head: Enzyme
Cuts after (C-terminal side of)
Pocket
rows: Asp at the bottom pairs with the + charge
Partly filled, so only small side chains fit

blocks.p: If a proline comes right after the cut site, cutting mostly fails. Proline's rigid ring keeps the substrate from bending into the transition state shape.

kcat (chemistry) goes up as the pH climbs toward 8, so the chemistry step needs a group that is **deprotonated**, so it can accept a proton. 1/Km (binding) drops at high pH, so binding needs a group that stays **protonated**. The overall rate peaks right around pH 8, the sweet spot where both are true. That fits chymotrypsin working in the small intestine.

blocks.tip: 1/Km going down means Km going up, which means worse binding. Don't flip that.

blocks.p: Inhibitors that bind the active site (like transition-state mimics) are specific, since active sites are where these enzymes differ the most. An allosteric inhibitor can hit both chymotrypsin and trypsin, because the site it binds is shared between them.

list: Genetic control: change how much enzyme gets made.
Reversible covalent modification: phosphorylation and similar.
Allosteric control: a molecule binds elsewhere to turn it up or down (think BPG and hemoglobin).
Zymogens: made inactive, switched on by a cut. Chymotrypsinogen gets cut, and active chymotrypsin can cut more of it (self-cleaving).

blocks.key: Chymotrypsin = aromatics, trypsin = Lys/Arg (Asp in pocket), elastase = small. Proline blocks. kcat wants deprotonated, binding wants protonated, peak near pH 8.

example.q: Design a pocket for a protease that cuts after Asp or Glu.
example.a: Make it positively charged (lined with Arg or Lys) so it pairs with the negative side chain, the mirror image of trypsin.

questions.question: Which are the four strategies enzymes use to lower activation energy? (Select all that apply)
options: Bringing the substrates close together (proximity)
Locking down random structural vibrations (Brownian motion)
Stabilizing the transition state and intermediates
Raising the temperature inside the active site pocket
Making the products more stable than they'd be without the enzyme
Holding the substrate in the right orientation
questions.explanation: Those four are straight from the slides. Enzymes never change product stability (that would change ΔG'°).

questions.question: Which strategies give enzymes the biggest rate boost (up to about 10^8-fold)?
options: Locking down vibrations and stabilizing the transition state
Bringing substrates close and holding them in the right orientation
Bringing substrates close and making the products more stable
Holding the right orientation and shifting the reaction's ΔG'°
questions.explanation: Proximity and orientation give a modest boost. Restricting Brownian motion and transition-state stabilization are the heavy hitters.

questions.question: In the peroxide demo, KI gave about a 100-fold boost, MnO2 about 1,000-fold, and pure catalase could give about 10^6-fold. What stayed the same in all three?
options: The activation energy, since all three are catalysts
The rate, once you correct for how much catalyst was added
The amount of heat given off every second of the reaction
The products and the overall energy change of the reaction
questions.explanation: Water and O2 were always the products. Catalysts change the path (the barrier), not where you end up.

questions.question: What does 'induced fit' mean for an enzyme?
options: The substrate changes shape to fit a rigid active site that never moves at all
The enzyme only binds its substrate after a cofactor has already filled the pocket
The enzyme fits the product best, which is why products release so slowly
The enzyme changes shape when substrate binds, pulling it toward the transition state
questions.explanation: Binding isn't a rigid lock and key. The enzyme moves around the substrate and helps strain it toward the transition state.

questions.question: Serine's -OH normally has a very high pKa. How does the catalytic triad turn it into a nucleophile at pH 7-8?
options: Asp's negative charge makes His want a proton; His pulls the H off Ser, leaving a reactive alkoxide
His's positive charge pushes a proton onto Asp, which then pulls the H off Ser to make an alkoxide
Ser hands its proton straight to Asp, while His holds the substrate in place for the attack
Asp attacks the carbonyl first, and then His and Ser stabilize the negative charge that forms
questions.explanation: The local environment shifts pKa values: next to Asp, His acts as a strong base and rips the proton off Ser.

questions.question: What is Asp102's main job in the catalytic triad?
options: Acting as the nucleophile that attacks the substrate's carbonyl directly
Giving a proton to the leaving amine so the first product can diffuse off
Binding the substrate's side chain so the right peptide bond lines up
Stabilizing the positive charge His picks up after it takes Ser's proton
questions.explanation: Asp never touches the substrate. It keeps His happy (protonated) so His can do the proton shuttling.

questions.question: What role(s) does His57 play during chymotrypsin catalysis? (Select all that apply)
options: General acid: gives a proton to the leaving amine as the first product breaks off
Nucleophile: attacks the carbonyl carbon of the peptide bond itself
General base: pulls the proton off Ser195 to make the nucleophile
Specificity: decides which side chain fits down in the pocket
General base again in phase 2: pulls a proton off the incoming water
questions.explanation: His is the proton shuttle. Ser is the nucleophile and the pocket handles specificity.

questions.question: What stabilizes the negative oxygen (oxyanion) in chymotrypsin's tetrahedral intermediate?
options: The positive charge on the protonated His side chain of the triad
Partial positive N-H groups from the protein backbone in the oxyanion hole
A bound Mg2+ ion sitting at the bottom of the specificity pocket
Positively charged Lys and Arg side chains lining the hydrophobic pocket
questions.explanation: He pointed this out on purpose: it's the backbone amides, not R groups, that make the oxyanion hole.

questions.question: Match chymotrypsin's active-site parts to their jobs.
options: Triad: prepares the nucleophile. Pocket: gives specificity. Oxyanion hole: stabilizes the intermediate
Triad: gives specificity. Pocket: prepares the nucleophile. Oxyanion hole: stabilizes the intermediate
Triad: stabilizes the intermediate. Pocket: gives specificity. Oxyanion hole: prepares the nucleophile
Triad: prepares the nucleophile. Pocket: stabilizes the intermediate. Oxyanion hole: gives specificity
questions.explanation: This exact matching shows up in almost every practice set. Memorize it cold.

questions.question: Which statements about serine protease active sites are true? (Select all that apply)
options: The oxyanion hole stabilizes the negative charge that forms on the substrate's carbonyl oxygen
The specificity pocket decides which residues the enzyme cuts after
The catalytic triad is made of the serine, the oxyanion hole, and the pocket
The serine nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon of the peptide bond
The oxyanion hole stabilizes the serine while it carries a negative charge
questions.explanation: The oxyanion is on the SUBSTRATE, not the serine. The triad is Ser, His, Asp.

questions.question: What is the 'acyl-enzyme intermediate' in chymotrypsin's mechanism?
options: The whole substrate held in the pocket by weak forces before any bond breaks at all
His57 covalently bonded to the substrate's amine half right after water comes in
The tetrahedral substrate held in the oxyanion hole by hydrogen bonds only
The substrate's carbonyl half covalently bonded to Ser195 after the amine half leaves
questions.explanation: End of phase 1: one product is gone and the other half of the peptide is stuck to Ser as an ester. Water releases it in phase 2.

questions.question: Put chymotrypsin's major events in order.
options: Water attacks, Ser attacks, oxyanion forms, amine half leaves, carboxyl half leaves, substrate binds
Substrate binds, water attacks, oxyanion forms, carboxyl half leaves, Ser attacks, amine half leaves
Substrate binds, Ser attacks, carboxyl half leaves, water attacks, oxyanion forms, amine half leaves
Substrate binds, Ser attacks, oxyanion forms, amine half leaves, water attacks, carboxyl half leaves
questions.explanation: Phase 1 (acylation) kicks out the amine half. Phase 2 (deacylation) uses water to kick out the carboxyl half.

questions.question: In phase 2 (deacylation), where does His57 get a proton from, now that Ser is already bonded to the substrate?
options: From a water molecule that slips into the space the first product left
From Asp102, which gives back the proton it took earlier in the cycle
From the backbone N-H groups of the oxyanion hole next to it
From the amine half of the peptide just before it leaves the site
questions.explanation: His still wants to be protonated, and Ser has nothing left to give, so it takes H from water. That makes the water oxygen the new attacker.

questions.question: Why does an inhibitor that gets through acylation but can't be deacylated count as a suicide inhibitor?
options: The covalent acyl-enzyme is more stable than letting go, so the enzyme stays stuck for good
It binds the oxyanion hole so tightly that substrate can never get back into the pocket again
It deacylates too fast, so the enzyme wears itself out after only a few rounds
It shifts the enzyme's ΔG'° so the reaction now runs backward for good
questions.explanation: Once it's covalently attached and won't come off, that enzyme molecule is permanently out of play.

questions.question: Chymotrypsin is handed the peptide ...Ala-Trp-Gly-Phe-Pro-Lys... Where does it cut?
options: After Trp and after Phe, since both are bulky aromatic residues
After Lys only, since chymotrypsin prefers positively charged side chains
Before Trp and before Phe, on the N-terminal side of each aromatic
After Trp only; the Phe is followed by Pro, which blocks the transition state
questions.explanation: Chymotrypsin cuts on the C-terminal side of aromatics, but a following proline makes things weird and blocks the cut.

questions.question: Why does a proline right after an aromatic residue keep chymotrypsin from cutting there?
options: Proline's rigid ring restricts the substrate so it can't bend into the transition state
Proline is positively charged, so it gets pushed right back out of the hydrophobic pocket
Proline's side chain bonds covalently to Ser195 and permanently kills the enzyme
Proline sits in the oxyanion hole and keeps the intermediate from forming
questions.explanation: Enzymes work by stabilizing the transition state. If the substrate can't get there, there's nothing to stabilize.

questions.question: Trypsin cuts after Lys and Arg. What sits at the bottom of its specificity pocket?
options: A lysine, whose positive charge repels everything but neutral side chains
An aspartate, whose negative charge pairs with the positive Lys or Arg
Nothing at all; the pocket is purely hydrophobic like chymotrypsin's
Two glycines that leave room for only tiny side chains like Ala
questions.explanation: Opposite charges attract. A negative Asp at the bottom is the perfect anchor for a long positive side chain.

questions.question: You want a serine protease that cuts after Asp or Glu. What pocket would you design?
options: A negatively charged pocket (lined with Asp or Glu) to pair with the negative side chain
A positively charged pocket (lined with Arg or Lys) to pair with the negative side chain
A large hydrophobic pocket lined with aromatics, just like chymotrypsin's pocket
A small pocket half-filled with bulky residues, just like elastase's pocket
questions.explanation: Flip trypsin's logic: a negative side chain wants a positive pocket. Like charges in the pocket would repel it.

questions.question: Elastase cuts after small residues like Ala. How is its pocket different?
options: An aspartate at the bottom attracts small positively charged residues
The pocket is extra large, so small residues slide fully inside it
Bulky residues partly fill the pocket, so only small side chains fit
There's no pocket at all, so elastase cuts at random spots
questions.explanation: Elastase basically fills in half the pocket. Same mechanism, smaller parking spot.

questions.question: Chymotrypsin, trypsin, and elastase share about 40% sequence identity, the same triad, and nearly the same fold, but cut different sites. What evolution story fits?
options: Convergent evolution: unrelated enzymes arrived at the same triad separately
Divergent evolution: they have unrelated folds but ended up with the same job
Convergent evolution: they started identical and slowly lost their shared triad
Divergent evolution: one ancestor branched into enzymes with new specificities
questions.explanation: High identity and the same structure but different jobs = divergent. Convergent is unrelated proteins landing on the same solution.

questions.question: kcat for chymotrypsin climbs as pH goes from about 6 to 8. Assuming general acid-base catalysis, what does the chemistry step need?
options: A group that must stay protonated (an amine) so it keeps its positive charge
A carboxyl that must stay protonated so it can hand its proton off
A group that must be deprotonated (an amine-type N) so it can accept a proton
A hydroxyl that must lose its proton on its own before substrate binds
questions.explanation: Activity rising as things get more basic means you need the deprotonated form. That's the base that pulls Ser's proton.

questions.question: 1/Km for chymotrypsin is high around pH 7-8 but falls at higher pH. What does binding need?
options: A deprotonated amine; at high pH more of it gets deprotonated, so binding improves
A protonated (positive) amine; at high pH it loses its proton and binding gets worse
A protonated carboxyl; at high pH it stays protonated, so binding gets better
No ionizable group; the drop is just the enzyme unfolding at high pH
questions.explanation: 1/Km falling means Km rising, which means weaker binding. So binding depends on a group that loses its proton at high pH.

questions.question: Why does chymotrypsin's overall activity peak right around pH 8?
options: It's where the catalysis group is deprotonated but the binding group is still protonated
It's the pKa of serine, so half the serines are deprotonated and ready to attack
It's the point where both the catalysis group and the binding group are fully deprotonated
It's the pH of the stomach, where chymotrypsin first gets cut out of its zymogen
questions.explanation: Two different groups, two different needs, one best pH. Chymotrypsin works in the small intestine.

questions.question: A transition-state mimic blocks chymotrypsin but not trypsin, while an allosteric inhibitor blocks both. Best explanation?
options: Active sites are where the two differ most, while the allosteric site is shared
Trypsin has no active site of its own, so only allosteric drugs can reach it
Allosteric inhibitors are always irreversible, so they hit any serine protease
Transition-state mimics only work on enzymes that cut after Lys or Arg
questions.explanation: Their mechanisms are nearly the same, but their pockets and transition states differ. A shared allosteric site doesn't care.

questions.question: Which are ways cells regulate enzyme activity? (Select all that apply)
options: Reversible covalent modification like phosphorylation
Changing how much of the enzyme gets made (genetic control)
Adding extra catalytic triads when demand for the enzyme is high
Allosteric binding of an activator or inhibitor (like BPG)
Cutting an inactive zymogen into its active form
Changing the enzyme's ΔG'° so the reaction direction flips
questions.explanation: Those four are the regulation list from the chymotrypsin lecture.

questions.question: Chymotrypsin is made as chymotrypsinogen. How does it get switched on?
options: A cut removes part of the chain; active chymotrypsin can then cut more (self-cleaving)
A kinase adds a phosphate to Ser195, which completes the catalytic triad
An allosteric activator binds and swings the oxyanion hole into its working position
It's made already fully active but kept quiet by the low pH of the small intestine
questions.explanation: Zymogens are switched on by proteolytic cleavage. Once some chymotrypsin is active, it helps activate the rest.

questions.question: Why do cells make proteases like chymotrypsin as inactive zymogens in the first place?
options: So they can be stored as phosphate reserves until the cell needs energy
So they don't chew up the cells that make them before they reach the gut
So their Km stays high until substrate is plentiful in the small intestine
So transition-state analogs can't inhibit them while they're being made
questions.explanation: A protease that's active from the start would digest its own factory. Making it inactive and cutting it on site is a safety switch.

lessons.title: Naming and drawing lipids
lessons.search: fatty acid nomenclature delta omega glycerophospholipid naming

blocks.p: Dr. Tracy calls the number system 'address notation.' It's how you'll name lipids on the exam. Common names you only need to recognize.

steps: Count every carbon, starting at the carboxyl carbon as carbon 1. That's X.
Count the double bonds. That's Y. Zero means saturated.
For each double bond, write the number of its FIRST carbon (the lower number), counting from the carboxyl end. That's the Δ list.
Assume cis unless told otherwise; natural lipids are cis.

blocks.p: Example: 18 carbons, double bonds starting at C9 and C12 = **18:2(Δ9,12)**, linoleic acid.

blocks.h: Omega: count from the other end

blocks.p: Omega is a class, not a full name. Start at the methyl end as carbon 1 and count to the first double bond you hit. Quick math: **omega number = total carbons minus the last Δ number**. 18:3(Δ9,12,15) is 18 - 15 = omega-3. Arachidonic acid 20:4(Δ5,8,11,14) is 20 - 14 = omega-6. Oleic 18:1(Δ9) is omega-9.

head: Triacylglycerol
Diacylglycerol (glycerophospholipid)
rows: 2 fatty acids + a polar head group
More complex end chain is C1; middle is always C2
Head group is ALWAYS C3, so the other end is C1
Cylinder, so it stacks into bilayers

blocks.p: Usually C1 holds a saturated chain and C2 holds an unsaturated one. A single-tail fatty acid is cone shaped and curls into micelles (that's soap).

Every glycerophospholipid head has a phosphate, which carries a negative charge. Choline and ethanolamine bring a positive nitrogen, so PC and PE are neutral overall. Serine, inositol, and plain H (phosphatidic acid) leave the lipid net negative. He'll give you the head-group table on the exam if you need to draw one.

steps: Draw glycerol as three carbons in a vertical line; label them 1, 2, 3 from top to bottom.
On C3, draw O, then a phosphate (P with two O's and one O-), then the choline on the far side.
On C1, draw an ester (O-C=O) and a 16-carbon zigzag with no double bonds. The C=O carbon is carbon 1 of that chain.
On C2, draw an ester and an 18-carbon zigzag. Count from the C=O carbon as 1 and put a cis double bond between carbons 9 and 10.
Check: C3 head, C1 saturated, C2 kinked.

blocks.h: Other lipids to recognize on sight

list: Sphingolipids: sphingosine backbone, head at C1, fatty acid joined by an amide (N) at C2, built-in carbon tail at C3. Myelin, gangliosides, and blood types A/B/O.
Ether lipids: an ether instead of an ester at C1. Less reactive, so they last longer.
Sterols (cholesterol): fused rings plus one -OH. Stiffens membranes; parent of steroid hormones.

blocks.key: Δ counts from the carboxyl carbon; omega counts from the methyl end. Head group is at C3 for glycerophospholipids. Phosphate = negative charge.

example.q: Name the omega class of 20:5(Δ5,8,11,14,17).

lessons.title: Saturation, fluidity, and signal lipids
lessons.search: membrane fluidity saturated unsaturated lipids flippase lipid raft

blocks.p: A cis double bond puts a kink in the tail. Kinked tails can't pack tightly, so they melt at lower temperatures and make membranes more fluid. Straight saturated tails pack tight, melt higher, and stiffen membranes. Bacon grease hardens; vegetable oil doesn't.

head: Environment
Organism wants
So it uses
rows: Membranes that don't get too floppy

blocks.p: Desaturation mostly changes **lateral** fluidity (sliding side to side). Lipids almost never flip vertically on their own, because the polar head would have to drag through the oily middle. Cholesterol packs between lipids and stiffens things.

list: FRAP: bleach a spot, watch fluorescence come back. Lipids and proteins slide around laterally.
Lateral movement is fast; flip-flop takes days unless an enzyme does it.
Flippases (outside to inside) and floppases (inside to outside) spend ATP to keep the two leaflets different. Scramblases just even things out.
Different leaflets and organelles have different lipid mixes, which is how proteins know where they are.
Fences: lipid rafts, big protein complexes, and cytoskeleton-anchored proteins all corral lipids.
Steroid hormones (from cholesterol) slip through membranes and bind receptors inside the nucleus.
Arachidonic acid (20 carbons) feeds cyclooxygenase (COX) to make prostaglandins for pain and inflammation. NSAIDs block COX.
Phospholipase C cuts PIP2 into DAG (stays in the membrane) and IP3 (goes into the cytosol). Both are second messengers.

blocks.key: More unsaturated = more kinks = lower melting point = more fluid. Lateral movement is easy; flip-flop needs enzymes.

example.q: Would a hot-spring bacterium have more or less desaturation than you?
example.a: Less. More saturated chains pack tighter and keep the membrane stable at high temperatures.

lessons.title: Getting across: transport and the ΔG math
lessons.search: electrochemical gradient membrane transport delta G equation

head: Type
Energy source
Example
rows: ATP hydrolysis right at the transporter
Another solute running down its gradient

blocks.p: Uniporter = one thing. Symporter = two things the same direction. Antiporter = two things opposite directions. Direction words are separate from energy words: a symporter can be passive or secondary active.

ΔG = RT ln(C2/C1) + ZFΔψ. C2 is where the ion is GOING, C1 is where it's COMING FROM. Z is its charge (+1, -1, +2). Δψ is the voltage where it's going minus where it's coming from. At 37 °C, RT is about 2.58 kJ/mol and F is about 96.5 kJ/(V·mol).

steps: Before any math, ask: does the concentration say go or stay? (High to low = negative term.)
Ask: does the charge say go or stay? (+ ion heading to a more negative side = negative term.)
Plug in, and make sure each term's sign matches what you predicted.
Add them. Negative total = favorable.

blocks.tip: He warned that he might report Δψ in a direction that doesn't match your move. Don't trust the sign blindly; reason it out.

example.q: K+: 140 mM inside, 4 mM outside, Δψ = -70 mV (inside negative), 37 °C. ΔG to move K+ OUT?
example.a: Concentration: 2.58 × ln(4/140) = -9.2 kJ/mol. Charge: +1 × 96.5 × (+0.070) = +6.8 kJ/mol (a + ion leaving a negative inside is uphill). Total ≈ -2.4 kJ/mol, slightly favorable.

example.q: Na+: 145 mM outside, 12 mM inside, same voltage. ΔG to move Na+ IN?
example.a: 2.58 × ln(12/145) = -6.4, plus 96.5 × (-0.070) = -6.8. Total ≈ -13.2 kJ/mol. Both terms say go, which is why Na+ is such a good battery for secondary transport.

list: K+ channels pass K+ but block the smaller Na+: the channel copies K+'s water shell exactly, so K+ can trade water for channel, but Na+ won't give up its shell.
Na+/K+ ATPase: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP, so the outside gets more positive (resting potential).
ABC transporters only move when ATP is hydrolyzed, a ratchet that can't run backward.
Drugs interact through transporters too: blocking OAT1 keeps other drugs in the blood longer.

blocks.key: ΔG = RT ln(C2/C1) + ZFΔψ, with 2 = destination. Predict both signs first, then calculate.

questions.question: An 18-carbon fatty acid has double bonds starting at carbons 9 and 12, counting the carboxyl carbon as C1. What's its address notation?
questions.explanation: Carbons : double bonds (Δ starting positions from the carboxyl end). This is linoleic acid.

questions.question: For Δ (address) notation, where do you start counting carbons?
options: At the carboxyl carbon, which counts as carbon 1
At the terminal methyl carbon, which counts as carbon 1
At the first carbon right after the carboxyl group
At whichever end is closer to the first double bond
questions.explanation: He was explicit: always start at the carboxyl group, and that carbon counts. Omega is the one that counts from the methyl end.

questions.question: What is the omega class of 18:3(Δ9,12,15)?
options: Omega-9
Omega-3
Omega-6
Omega-15
questions.explanation: 18 - 15 = 3. The TA slide stressed it's just 'omega-3,' not 'omega-3,6,9.'

questions.question: Arachidonic acid is 20:4(Δ5,8,11,14). Which omega class is it?
options: Omega-3
Omega-5
Omega-4
Omega-6
questions.explanation: 20 - 14 = 6. The last double bond starts 6 carbons in from the methyl end.

questions.question: A 16-carbon fatty acid with one double bond is an omega-7. What's its address notation?
questions.explanation: Omega = total - Δ, so Δ = 16 - 7 = 9. That's palmitoleic acid.

questions.question: Which two fatty acids are 'essential' (you have to eat them because you can't make them)?
options: Palmitic and stearic acid
Linoleic and linolenic acid
Oleic and palmitoleic acid
Arachidonic and stearic acid
questions.explanation: Those two are the essential fatty acids from lecture. Everything else your body can build.

questions.question: For a glycerophospholipid (a diacylglycerol), which glycerol position holds the polar head group?
options: Position 3
Position 1
Position 2
Whichever end has the longer chain
questions.explanation: Head group is always C3 for glycerophospholipids. (Sphingolipids flip it and put the head at C1, just to be fun.)

questions.question: A glycerophospholipid has: C1 = 16 carbons, saturated; C2 = 18 carbons with one double bond starting at C9; head group = choline. What's its address name?
options: 1-18:1(Δ9), 2-16:0, 3-phosphocholine
1-16:0, 2-18:1(Δ9), 3-phosphocholine
1-16:0, 2-18:1(Δ9), 1-phosphocholine
1-phosphocholine, 2-18:1(Δ9), 3-16:0
questions.explanation: Head at 3, then the chain next to it is 2, the far one is 1. This is the beef-membrane lipid from the review activity.

questions.question: You're drawing 1-16:0, 2-18:1(Δ9), 3-phosphocholine by hand. Where does the double bond go?
options: Between carbons 9 and 10 of the chain on glycerol C1, counting its C=O carbon as 1
Between carbons 9 and 10 of the chain on glycerol C2, counting from its methyl end
Between carbons 9 and 10 of the chain on glycerol C2, counting its C=O carbon as 1
Between glycerol carbons 2 and 3, right next to where the choline head is attached
questions.explanation: The 18:1 chain sits at position 2. Δ9 means the double bond starts at carbon 9 counting from the carbonyl carbon.

questions.question: In a typical membrane glycerophospholipid, which chain usually sits at C1 vs C2?
options: C1 is usually unsaturated and C2 is usually saturated
Both are usually unsaturated to keep the membrane fluid
C1 is usually saturated and C2 is usually unsaturated
Both are usually saturated to keep the membrane sealed
questions.explanation: Not a hard rule, but it's the general pattern he gave. The PS example in class (unsaturated at C1) was called out as an exception.

questions.question: When naming a triacylglycerol, how do you decide which end is C1?
options: The most complex chain anywhere is C1, even if it sits in the middle position
The more complex end chain (longer or more unsaturated) is C1; the middle is always C2
The shortest chain is always C1, so the whole name reads from the short chain to the long one
The head-group end is always C1, the same rule as for a diacylglycerol
questions.explanation: Only the two ends compete for number 1. The middle carbon of glycerol is always 2.

questions.question: Why are triacylglycerols such good energy storage?
options: They pack tightly with no water, giving over twice the energy per gram of carbs or protein
They're heavily hydrated, so each gram of stored fat also stores extra water for later
They carry a charged head group, which lets them pack into tight, stackable bilayers
They're mostly oxidized carbon, so breaking them down gives off no CO2 at all
questions.explanation: No water needed, hydrophobic packing, and more than 2x the energy of the same mass of protein or carbohydrate.

questions.question: Why do single-tail fatty acids form micelles, while two-tail phospholipids form bilayers?
options: One tail is more hydrophilic, so it hides in a ball; two tails can stay in the water
One tail makes a cone that curls into a ball; two tails make a cylinder that stacks flat
Two tails carry more charge, so they repel each other into flat sheets instead of balls
One tail can't bind cholesterol, so it can't ever form a flat, stable sheet
questions.explanation: Shape decides packing. Cone = micelle (soap). Cylinder = bilayer (membranes, liposomes).

questions.question: Why does phosphatidic acid (just H at the X position) carry a negative charge?
options: The glycerol backbone loses a proton from one of its hydroxyls
The phosphate in the head group is negatively charged at pH 7
The carboxyl ends of both fatty acids stay deprotonated
The double bonds in the tails pull electron density into the head
questions.explanation: The phosphate is the source of the negative charge on every glycerophospholipid. A neutral lipid needs a positive group (like choline) to balance it.

questions.question: Which head groups give a glycerophospholipid a net charge of ZERO at pH 7? (Select all that apply)
options: Just H (phosphatidic acid)
Serine (phosphatidylserine)
Inositol (phosphatidylinositol)
Choline (phosphatidylcholine)
Ethanolamine (phosphatidylethanolamine)
questions.explanation: Choline and ethanolamine have a positive nitrogen that cancels the phosphate. Serine, inositol, and H leave it net negative.

questions.question: A lipid has an amide (N) link at C2, a long built-in carbon chain at C3, and its head group at C1. What is it?
options: A glycerophospholipid
A sphingolipid
An ether lipid
A triacylglycerol
questions.explanation: That's the sphingosine backbone. You need to recognize sphingolipids, not draw them.

questions.question: Ether lipids (like the blood-pressure-lowering one from class) last a long time at low doses, mostly because...
options: Ethers carry extra charge, so they bind their receptors much more tightly
Ethers are less reactive than esters, so they get broken down more slowly
Ethers are more polar than esters, so they stay dissolved in blood longer
Ethers form micelles that the liver has no way of breaking apart
questions.explanation: Ester links are more reactive. Swap in an ether and the molecule is more stable, so a little goes a long way.

questions.question: What changes when a fatty acid gets a cis double bond (desaturation)? (Select all that apply)
options: Its melting temperature drops
Membranes made from it get more fluid
It becomes much less hydrophobic
It gets a kink that keeps it from packing tightly
It flips across the bilayer vertically much more easily
questions.explanation: Desaturation changes flexibility, packing, and melting point. The tail is still hydrophobic, and flip-flop is still hard.

questions.question: Why does bacon grease harden as it cools while vegetable oil stays liquid?
options: Bacon fat has more cis double bonds, and the kinks lock its chains together as it cools
Bacon fat is richer in straight saturated chains that pack tight; oil's cis kinks keep it loose
Bacon fat has much shorter chains, and shorter chains always have the higher melting points
Vegetable oil has more carboxyl groups, which hydrogen bond with water and stay liquid
questions.explanation: Saturated = straight = tight packing = higher melting point. That's the same reason steak fat hardens on your plate.

questions.question: Compared to human membranes, bacteria living in a hot spring would have...
options: Less desaturation, so the chains pack tighter and the membrane stays stable at high heat
More desaturation, so the membrane stays fluid enough to function at high heat
The same desaturation, since high temperature only affects proteins and never the lipids
More desaturation, so lateral fluidity drops while vertical fluidity goes up
questions.explanation: Heat makes membranes too fluid, so you fight it with more saturated lipids (higher melting point).

questions.question: A fish living in near-freezing water would most likely...
options: Raise the share of saturated lipids so its membranes don't get too fluid
Raise the share of unsaturated lipids so its membranes don't get too stiff
Swap its phospholipids for triacylglycerols to keep its membranes warm
Remove all its cholesterol and replace it with extra sphingolipids
questions.explanation: Cold makes membranes stiff, so you want more kinks to keep them fluid. The TA review asked this exact idea.

questions.question: Desaturation mostly changes which kind of membrane movement?
options: Lateral fluidity, since polar heads can't easily cross the oily middle anyway
Vertical (flip-flop) movement, since the kinks open a path straight across
Solubility in water, since the kinks expose the tails to the water outside
Neither one; desaturation only changes melting point, not how lipids move
questions.explanation: This was a clicker question. Side-to-side gets looser; flipping is still blocked by the hydrophobic core.

questions.question: What does cholesterol do to a membrane?
options: Adds kinks between phospholipids and makes it more fluid
Pulls water into the bilayer and swells the oily core
Carries a negative charge that sets the membrane potential
Packs between phospholipids and stiffens the membrane
questions.explanation: Cholesterol is a rigid ring system. Too much makes membranes too stiff.

questions.question: How do steroid hormones like estrogen reach receptors inside the nucleus?
options: They're carried across by GPCRs, which then release them directly into the nucleus
They bind a surface receptor that sends cAMP into the nucleus to act in their place
They're charged at pH 7, so ion channels pull them into the cell and nucleus
They diffuse through membranes, and high-affinity receptors catch them even at low levels
questions.explanation: Steroids diffuse into and through membranes by equilibrium. Their receptors have very high affinity, so even low inside concentrations work.

questions.question: How do NSAIDs like ibuprofen cut pain and inflammation?
options: They block phospholipase C, which turns PIP2 into the pain signal IP3
They block cholesterol from being turned into swelling-causing steroids
They block cyclooxygenase, which turns arachidonic acid into prostaglandins
They block flippases so pain lipids stay stuck on the outer membrane
questions.explanation: Arachidonic acid (a 20-carbon eicosanoid precursor) feeds COX to make prostaglandins. Block COX, block the signal. COX-2 was discovered at BYU.

questions.question: When phospholipase C cuts PIP2, what are the two pieces and where does each go?
options: IP3 stays in the membrane; DAG heads into the cytosol
PIP3 stays in the membrane; DAG heads into the nucleus
DAG stays in the membrane; IP3 heads into the cytosol
Both pieces stay in the membrane and recruit PKA there
questions.explanation: DAG is the greasy two-tailed part, so it stays put. IP3 is the polar sugar-phosphate head, so it diffuses into the cytosol.

questions.question: In the fluorescence-bleaching experiment (FRAP), a bleached spot on the membrane slowly glowed again. What did that show?
options: The dye slowly repairs itself over time, so the membrane is actually rigid
Lipids and proteins move laterally, so unbleached ones drifted into the spot
Lipids flipped up from the inner leaflet to refill the outer leaflet
The cell built new membrane at that spot to replace the bleached lipids
questions.explanation: Fluorescence coming back means stuff moved in from next door. That's the evidence for the fluid mosaic model.

questions.question: Which can fence lipids into small regions of the membrane? (Select all that apply)
options: Large protein complexes that lipids have to go all the way around
Hydrogen bonds between neighboring fatty acid tails
Lipid rafts of similar (like longer) lipids that cluster together
The negative charge on cholesterol
Proteins anchored to the cytoskeleton
questions.explanation: All three showed up in the lipid-tracking clicker question. Brownian motion drives the movement; structure restricts it.

questions.question: Flippases and floppases spend ATP. Why does the cell bother?
options: To keep the two leaflets different, which tells proteins which membrane they're on
To make flip-flop faster than lateral movement, so all the lipids mix evenly
To pump ions out of the cell along with every lipid they move across the bilayer
To break down old lipids so brand new ones can be made in their place
questions.explanation: The two leaflets (and different organelles) have different lipid mixes on purpose. Scramblases, which just even things out, don't need ATP.

questions.question: Which statement about lipid movement is correct?
options: Lateral movement is fast; flip-flop is so slow it needs enzymes
Flip-flop is fast; lateral movement is so slow it needs enzymes
Both are fast, since Brownian motion moves lipids around freely
Both are slow, since proteins hold every lipid firmly in place
questions.explanation: Lateral: thousands of angstroms per second. Flip-flop: days, unless a flippase or floppase helps.

questions.question: O2 crosses a membrane on its own, but Na+ needs a channel. Why?
options: O2 is pumped across by the Na+/K+ ATPase, while Na+ can only diffuse
O2 rides on hemoglobin sitting in the membrane, which carries it across
O2 is small and nonpolar, so the oily core doesn't stop it; Na+ is charged
Na+ is bigger than O2, so it can't squeeze between the lipid tails
questions.explanation: The hydrophobic middle is the barrier. Small nonpolar molecules slip through; charged ions need help.

questions.question: Which describe secondary active transport? (Select all that apply)
options: It can be a symporter (same direction) or an antiporter (opposite directions)
It only works through open ion channels
It burns ATP right at the transporter to move each solute
The Na+-glucose symporter is an example
One solute moves down its gradient to drag another up its gradient
questions.explanation: Secondary active borrows energy from another gradient. Direction (sym vs anti) is a separate question from energy (passive vs active).

questions.question: A 'funicular' (a train going downhill pulls another train uphill) is an analogy for which transporter?
options: A secondary active antiporter: one goes down its gradient as the other goes up the other way
A primary active uniporter: ATP drives a single solute up its gradient all by itself
An ion channel: ions simply flow down their own gradient in whichever direction they want
A facilitated uniporter: one solute moves down its gradient with no coupling at all
questions.explanation: Downhill pays for uphill, and they move in opposite directions. That's coupled, secondary active, antiport.

questions.question: How does an ABC transporter avoid running backward when its cargo is piled up on the far side?
options: It closes a gate behind the cargo that only a phosphatase can open again
It only moves when ATP is hydrolyzed, which acts like a ratchet that turns one way
Its cargo binds the far side so weakly that it can never come back through
It uses the membrane potential to push the cargo back in if it starts leaking out
questions.explanation: This was a clicker question: ATP hydrolysis gates the motion, so the Brownian ratchet only runs forward.

questions.question: Na+ is 145 mM outside and 12 mM inside. Δψ = -70 mV (inside negative), 37 °C. What is ΔG for moving Na+ INTO the cell? (ΔG = RT ln(C2/C1) + ZFΔψ)
options: -13.2 kJ/mol
+0.3 kJ/mol
-6.4 kJ/mol
+13.2 kJ/mol
questions.explanation: Concentration: 2.58 × ln(12/145) = -6.4. Charge: (+1)(96.5)(-0.070) = -6.8. Both favor moving in, total -13.2. Getting +0.3 means the voltage sign got flipped.

questions.question: K+ is 140 mM inside and 4 mM outside. Δψ = -70 mV (inside negative), 37 °C. What is ΔG for moving K+ OUT of the cell?
options: -15.9 kJ/mol
+2.4 kJ/mol
-9.2 kJ/mol
-2.4 kJ/mol
questions.explanation: Concentration: 2.58 × ln(4/140) = -9.2 (favorable). Charge: a + ion leaving a negative inside is uphill, +6.8. Net -2.4. This is the practice-question setup.

questions.question: Cl- is 110 mM outside and 10 mM inside, Δψ = -70 mV (inside negative), 37 °C. Is moving Cl- INTO the cell favorable?
options: Barely not: ΔG ≈ +0.6 kJ/mol, since the negative inside pushes back on the anion
Yes: ΔG ≈ -12.9 kJ/mol, since both concentration and charge favor moving in
Yes: ΔG ≈ -6.2 kJ/mol, since only the concentration term ever matters for anions
No: ΔG ≈ +12.9 kJ/mol, since both concentration and charge oppose moving in
questions.explanation: Concentration says in (-6.2). But Z = -1 heading into a negative inside is uphill: (-1)(96.5)(-0.070) = +6.8. Net about +0.6.

questions.question: Before plugging in numbers, Dr. Tracy says to sanity-check signs. For K+ moving OUT of a cell (high K+ inside, inside negative), what signs should the two terms have?
options: Concentration term positive (high to low), charge term negative (+ ion leaving a negative inside)
Both terms negative, since K+ always leaves cells on its own
Concentration term negative (high to low), charge term positive (+ ion leaving a negative inside)
Both terms positive, since moving any ion out of a cell costs energy
questions.explanation: Downhill concentration = negative. A positive ion leaving the negative side it's attracted to = uphill = positive. Then check your math matches.

questions.question: Glucose (uncharged) is 5 mM outside and 20 mM inside, 37 °C. What's ΔG to bring more glucose IN, and could Na+ coming in (ΔG = -13.2 kJ/mol) pay for it?
options: -3.6 kJ/mol; no coupling needed, since glucose flows in on its own
+3.6 kJ/mol; yes, coupling to Na+ makes it about -9.6 kJ/mol overall
+3.6 kJ/mol; no, since an uncharged solute can't be coupled to an ion
+16.8 kJ/mol; no, since the Na+ gradient is too small to cover it
questions.explanation: No charge term for glucose: 2.58 × ln(20/5) = +3.6. Add the Na+ move: -13.2 + 3.6 = -9.6. That's how the Na+-glucose symporter works.

questions.question: K+ is bigger than Na+, yet K+ channels let K+ through and keep Na+ out. How?
options: The channel pore is too narrow for Na+ but just wide enough for the bigger K+ ion to pass
The channel is lined with negative charge that only attracts the more charged K+
Any Na+ that slips into the pore gets pumped back out by the channel using ATP
The channel mimics K+'s water shell, so K+ swaps water for channel but Na+ keeps its shell
questions.explanation: Na+'s water cage is actually bigger, and the channel can't take it off. Still passive diffusion, just very selective.

questions.question: The Na+/K+ ATPase moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP. What does running it nonstop do?
options: Makes the inside more positive than the outside, which fires an action potential
Moves equal charge both ways, so it changes concentrations but not the voltage
Uses the Na+ gradient to make ATP, so it recharges the cell's batteries
Makes the outside more positive than the inside, helping set the resting potential
questions.explanation: Three positive charges out for every two in. Net positive charge piles up outside.

questions.question: A patient on furosemide (which blocks the OAT1 transporter) also takes an antibiotic that OAT1 normally pulls out of the blood. What happens?
options: The antibiotic clears faster, since furosemide speeds up every transporter
Nothing changes, since drug interactions only ever happen through direct chemical reactions
The antibiotic turns furosemide into an inactive form inside kidney cells
The antibiotic sticks around in the blood longer, even though the two drugs never react
questions.explanation: This is why doctors ask about every medication. Drugs can interact through transport, not just chemistry.

questions.question: Different CFTR mutations all cause cystic fibrosis. Which kinds of defects did lecture list? (Select all that apply)
options: The channel never gets made
The channel moves chloride too fast and dries out the mucus
The channel works but there isn't enough of it
The channel gets made but never reaches the membrane
The channel reaches the membrane but doesn't work right
questions.explanation: All four end in too little chloride moving. Which one it is changes the treatment you'd pick.

lessons.title: The seven principles of signaling
lessons.search: signal transduction specificity amplification modularity desensitization

blocks.p: Signaling is reception (a ligand hits a receptor), transduction (the message gets passed and amplified inside), and response (something changes: genes, enzymes, metabolism). He wants you to spot the seven principles inside any pathway he shows you.

head: Principle
Plain meaning
Example from class
rows: A receptor recognizes its signal and triggers its response
Only cells with the receptor respond
Responds to tiny amounts of signal (low Kd)
Black curve vs gray curve: lower Kd = more sensitive
One signal turns on many downstream molecules
Swap in different parts to get different responses (USB port)
Shc vs IRS on the insulin receptor
GRK2 + β-arrestin pull the GPCR inside
Combine inputs (AND/OR gates) or split one signal many ways (pleiotropy)
Epinephrine: heart rate up AND liver dumps glucose
Remover sits next to the receptor for fast on/off
Scaffolds in vision; PP2A next to PKA

blocks.tip: Affinity and cooperativity are NOT on the list. A practice question used affinity as the trap answer.
